solution:
Chlorination of methane is a free radical chain reaction. In the chain-termination step two methyl free radicals, produced during propagation, combine with each other:

Initiation: \(\text{Cl}-\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\,\dot{\text{C}}\text{l}\)

Propagation: \(\text{CH}_4 + \dot{\text{C}}\text{l} \rightarrow \dot{\text{C}}\text{H}_3 + \text{HCl}\)

Termination: \(\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}_3 + \dot{\text{C}}\text{H}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_3\)

Hence ethane is formed as a minor product of the termination step, in which two methyl radicals couple.

(a) \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\): the longest chain through the double bond is four carbons, with a methyl on C-2 — 2-Methylbut-2-ene.

(b) \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3\): five carbons; numbering from the \(\text{CH}_2=\) end gives the double bond 1 and the triple bond 3 — Pent-1-en-3-yne.

(c) The bond-line drawing is a straight chain of four carbons with double bonds on the first and third links — Buta-1,3-diene.

(d) \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\): a four-carbon chain with the double bond at C-1 and the ring at C-4 — 4-Phenylbut-1-ene.

(e) A benzene ring carrying \(-\text{OH}\) and, on the neighbouring carbon, \(-\text{CH}_3\). The \(-\text{OH}\) group takes C-1 — 2-Methylphenol.

(f) The central carbon carries a pentyl chain, a butyl chain and a \(-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) group. The longest chain runs pentyl-central-butyl, i.e. ten carbons, and the central carbon is C-5 counting from the butyl end — 5-(2-Methylpropyl)decane (5-isobutyldecane).

(g) \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\): the parent chain is ten carbons. Numbering from the \(\text{CH}_2=\) end gives double bonds at 1, 5, 8 (against 2, 5, 9 from the other end) and the ethyl group at C-4 — 4-Ethyldeca-1,5,8-triene.

Answers: (a) 2-Methylbut-2-ene (b) Pent-1-en-3-yne (c) Buta-1,3-diene (d) 4-Phenylbut-1-ene (e) 2-Methylphenol (f) 5-(2-Methylpropyl)decane (g) 4-Ethyldeca-1,5,8-triene.

[Textbook error in a drawn structure, affecting the picture rather than the answer. For part (a)(ii) the key draws \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\), in which the second carbon is shown carrying two hydrogens AND a double bond — five bonds to one carbon, which cannot exist. The NAME the key prints beside it, But-2-ene, is correct, and corresponds to \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\); one hydrogen has simply been left on the drawn structure. The answer below gives the tetravalent structure.] (a) \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\) with one double bond — three structural isomers:

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) But-1-ene

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\) But-2-ene

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\) 2-Methylprop-1-ene

(b) \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\) with one triple bond — three structural isomers:

\(\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) Pent-1-yne

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) Pent-2-yne

\(\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_3\) 3-Methylbut-1-yne

But-2-ene additionally exists as cis and trans geometrical isomers, which are stereoisomers rather than structural isomers.

Ozonolysis cleaves the \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) bond and puts an oxygen on each of the two carbons, so each doubly bonded carbon becomes an aldehyde if it carries an H and a ketone if it does not.

(i) Pent-2-ene, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\): Ethanal and Propanal.

(ii) 3,4-Dimethylhept-3-ene, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\): Butan-2-one and Pentan-2-one.

(iii) 2-Ethylbut-1-ene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\): Methanal and Pentan-3-one.

(iv) 1-Phenylbut-1-ene, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\): Benzaldehyde and Propanal.

Ozonolysis is reversed by joining the two carbonyl carbons through a double bond.

Ethanal is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}\), so one carbon of the double bond carries \(\text{CH}_3\) and H.

Pentan-3-one is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{CO}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\), so the other carbon carries two ethyl groups.

Joining them:

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\)

The longest chain through the double bond is five carbons with the double bond at C-2 and an ethyl group at C-3.

Structure of 'A': \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\); IUPAC name: 3-Ethylpent-2-ene.

Three \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) sigma bonds mean a chain of four carbon atoms, and eight \(\text{C}-\text{H}\) sigma bonds mean eight hydrogens, so 'A' is \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\) with one \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) (the single \(\pi\) bond).

Ozonolysis gives two moles of the SAME aldehyde, so the double bond is symmetrically substituted and each carbon of it carries one H.

Molar mass 44 u corresponds to \(\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}\) (ethanal, \(24 + 4 + 16 = 44\)).

Two ethanal molecules joined at their carbonyl carbons give \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\).

IUPAC name of 'A': But-2-ene.

[Textbook answer-key error in a name the key VOLUNTEERS — the structure it draws is correct, and the structure is all this question asks for. The key names the compound \(4\)-Ethylhex-3-ene. Numbering the six-carbon chain from either end puts the double bond at C-3, so that criterion ties and the tie is broken by giving the SUBSTITUENT the lower locant: the ethyl group is C-3 from one end and C-4 from the other, so the preferred name is \(3\)-Ethylhex-3-ene. The book applies this same tiebreak correctly elsewhere in the chapter, at Problem 9.7(iv), which is what shows this to be a slip rather than a house convention.] Propanal is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}\), so one carbon of the double bond carries an ethyl group and an H. Pentan-3-one is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{CO}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\), so the other carries two ethyl groups. Joining the two carbonyl carbons by a double bond:

Structural formula of the alkene: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\)

(Its IUPAC name is 3-Ethylhex-3-ene.)

[Textbook answer-key error, self-refuting on the equation's own atom balance. Part (c) is printed \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}(g) + \tfrac{17}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2(g) + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\), which cannot balance: five carbons on the left cannot give six \(\text{CO}_2\) on the right. Every other atom already balances for \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\) — hydrogen \(10 \rightarrow 5\text{H}_2\text{O}\), oxygen \(17 \rightarrow 12 + 5\) — so the formula is a misprint for hexyne, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\), and the coefficients the key prints are the correct ones for it. The answer below uses \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\).] Complete combustion converts every carbon to \(\text{CO}_2\) and every two hydrogens to one \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

(i) Butane, \(\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\): \(2\,\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + 13\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\,\text{CO}_2 + 10\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(ii) Pentene, \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\): \(2\,\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + 15\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 10\,\text{CO}_2 + 10\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iii) Hexyne, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\): \(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + 17\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 12\,\text{CO}_2 + 10\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iv) Toluene, \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\): \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_8 + 9\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 7\,\text{CO}_2 + 4\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Hex-2-ene is \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\). The two doubly bonded carbons each carry an H and an alkyl group, so geometrical isomerism is possible.

In the cis isomer the \(\text{CH}_3\) and \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\) groups lie on the same side of the double bond and the two H atoms on the other side.

In the trans isomer the \(\text{CH}_3\) and \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\) groups lie on opposite sides, one H accompanying each.

In the cis form the two \(\text{C}-\text{alkyl}\) bond dipoles point to the same side and add to give a net dipole moment; in the trans form they point in opposite directions and very nearly cancel, so the trans isomer is almost non-polar. Stronger dipole-dipole attraction in the cis form means more energy is needed to separate its molecules.

Hence cis-hex-2-ene has the higher boiling point.

Benzene is not a molecule with three fixed double bonds; it is a resonance hybrid of the two equivalent Kekule structures, so its six \(\pi\) electrons are completely delocalised over all six carbon atoms in two ring-shaped clouds above and below the planar ring.

The evidence for this is that all six carbon-carbon bonds are of the same length, 139 pm, which lies between a normal single bond (154 pm) and a normal double bond (134 pm).

Because the ring is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated and holds \(4n+2 = 6\) \(\pi\) electrons (Huckel's rule with \(n = 1\)), the delocalisation is complete and releases a large resonance (delocalisation) energy of about \(150\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

This resonance stabilisation is what makes benzene extraordinarily stable, and it is why benzene prefers substitution (which preserves the delocalised sextet) to addition (which would destroy it).

(i) The six-membered ring carries two ring double bonds and a third double bond that points OUT of the ring to the \(=\text{CH}_2\) group. The carbon opposite the exocyclic group is \(sp^3\) (a \(\text{CH}_2\)) and has no p orbital, so the ring of p orbitals is broken and delocalisation cannot go all the way round. In addition the ring itself holds only 4 \(\pi\) electrons, which is \(4n\) and not \((4n+2)\). Hence not aromatic.

(ii) In cyclopentadiene one ring carbon is \(sp^3\) hybridised (the \(\text{CH}_2\) group) and carries no p orbital, so the cyclic conjugation is interrupted and the four \(\pi\) electrons cannot be delocalised over the whole ring. Four is also \(4n\), not \((4n+2)\). Hence not aromatic.

(iii) Cyclooctatetraene has eight \(\pi\) electrons, which is \(4n\) with \(n = 2\) and so fails Huckel's rule. To avoid the strain of a planar eight-membered ring the molecule adopts a non-planar tub shape, so adjacent p orbitals are not parallel and cannot overlap continuously. Hence not aromatic.

[Textbook answer-key errors, and the first is self-refuting on the key's own reaction scheme. In part (ii) the key's final product is DRAWN as 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene — a bromine where the nitro group belongs. Its own preceding step nitrates benzene with conc. \(\text{HNO}_3\)/conc. \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) to give nitrobenzene, and no bromine-bearing reagent appears anywhere in the sequence, so the bromine cannot have come from the route the key itself draws; the product of that route is 1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene. Confirmed at 5x magnification on the printed page. Secondary, in part (iii): the key prescribes DILUTE \(\text{HNO}_3\) and DILUTE \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) for a ring nitration, where its own parts (i) and (ii) and the chapter's own text all use the CONCENTRATED acids. The answer below uses the concentrated reagents.] The order of the two steps is decided by the directive influence of the first group introduced.

(i) \(p\)-Nitrobromobenzene: brominate first, because \(-\text{Br}\) is ortho, para directing.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. FeBr}_3]{\text{Br}_2} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 333\,\text{K}]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} p\text{-}\text{O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{Br}\)

(ii) \(m\)-Nitrochlorobenzene: nitrate first, because \(-\text{NO}_2\) is meta directing.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 333\,\text{K}]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. FeCl}_3]{\text{Cl}_2} m\text{-}\text{O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{Cl}\)

(iii) \(p\)-Nitrotoluene: alkylate first, because \(-\text{CH}_3\) is ortho, para directing.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3]{\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 333\,\text{K}]{\text{conc. HNO}_3} p\text{-}\text{O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_3\)

(iv) Acetophenone: a single Friedel-Crafts acylation.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3]{\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + \text{HCl}\)

In (i) and (iii) the para isomer is separated from the ortho isomer formed alongside it.

Number the chain of the alkane \(\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2\) as C-1 to C-5 from the left. A carbon is primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary according to how many OTHER carbon atoms it is bonded to.

Primary (\(1^\circ\)) carbons — bonded to one carbon each, 3 H atoms each. There are five of them: C-1, the two \(\text{CH}_3\) groups on C-3 and the two \(\text{CH}_3\) groups on C-5.

Secondary (\(2^\circ\)) carbons — bonded to two carbons each, 2 H atoms each. There are two: C-2 and C-4.

Tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) carbon — bonded to three carbons, 1 H atom. There is one: C-5.

(C-3 is bonded to four carbons and is therefore quaternary, with no H atom at all.)

Summary: \(1^\circ\) — five carbons, 3 H each; \(2^\circ\) — two carbons, 2 H each; \(3^\circ\) — one carbon, 1 H.

Boiling point of an alkane is governed by the strength of the van der Waals (London) forces between its molecules, and these increase with the surface area over which neighbouring molecules can touch.

Branching makes a molecule more compact and more nearly spherical, which reduces its surface area, weakens the intermolecular forces and therefore LOWERS the boiling point.

For the same molecular formula \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\): pentane 309 K, 2-methylbutane 301 K, 2,2-dimethylpropane 282.5 K — the boiling point falls as branching increases.

In the ABSENCE of peroxide the addition is electrophilic and ionic, and follows Markovnikov's rule.

\(\text{H}^{+}\) adds first, and it adds to the terminal carbon because that gives the more stable SECONDARY carbocation:

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3\) (secondary, stabilised by two alkyl groups) in preference to \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\) (primary).

\(\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CHBr}-\text{CH}_3\), 2-bromopropane.

In the PRESENCE of benzoyl peroxide the addition is a free radical chain reaction (peroxide or Kharasch effect) and the orientation is reversed.

Initiation: \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO})_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}\dot{\text{O}} \rightarrow 2\,\dot{\text{C}}_6\text{H}_5 + 2\,\text{CO}_2\); \(\dot{\text{C}}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{H}-\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \dot{\text{B}}\text{r}\)

Propagation: here it is \(\dot{\text{B}}\text{r}\), not \(\text{H}^{+}\), that adds first, and it adds to the terminal carbon because that gives the more stable SECONDARY free radical:

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \dot{\text{B}}\text{r} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) (secondary) in preference to \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CHBr}-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\) (primary)

\(\text{CH}_3-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{H}-\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \dot{\text{B}}\text{r}\), 1-bromopropane.

So the two products differ because in the ionic route the hydrogen adds first and in the radical route the bromine adds first, and in each case the FIRST species adds so as to leave the more stable secondary intermediate. The peroxide effect is seen only with HBr: the H-Cl bond is too strong to be broken by the radical, and iodine radicals prefer to combine with each other rather than add to the double bond.

\(o\)-Xylene is a resonance hybrid of two Kekule structures, and each of them would give a different set of ozonolysis products.

In one Kekule structure the two methyl-bearing carbons are joined by a double bond. Cleaving the three ring double bonds of that structure gives one molecule of butane-2,3-dione, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-\text{COCH}_3\), and two molecules of glyoxal (ethanedial), \(\text{OHC}-\text{CHO}\).

In the other Kekule structure the two methyl-bearing carbons are joined by a single bond. Cleaving that structure gives two molecules of 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal), \(\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-\text{CHO}\), and one molecule of glyoxal.

What is actually obtained is a MIXTURE of all three dicarbonyl compounds — glyoxal, 2-oxopropanal and butane-2,3-dione.

If \(o\)-xylene had a single fixed structure only one of the two sets could ever form. The appearance of all three products together shows that \(o\)-xylene (and hence benzene) is not one static structure but a hybrid oscillating between the two Kekule forms, which is exactly what the Kekule structure of benzene, taken together with resonance, requires.

Decreasing order of acidic behaviour: Ethyne > Benzene > \(n\)-Hexane.

The acidity of a \(\text{C}-\text{H}\) bond depends on the hybridisation of the carbon holding it, because the s orbital keeps electrons closer to the nucleus than a p orbital does. The greater the s character of the hybrid orbital, the more electronegative that carbon is, the more firmly it holds the electron pair left behind, and the more easily the hydrogen leaves as \(\text{H}^{+}\).

Ethyne: carbon is \(sp\) hybridised, 50% s character.

Benzene: carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised, 33.3% s character.

\(n\)-Hexane: carbon is \(sp^3\) hybridised, 25% s character.

Hence the carbanion left behind is most stable for ethyne and least stable for \(n\)-hexane, giving the order above.

Benzene has six delocalised \(\pi\) electrons spread in clouds above and below the plane of the ring, so the ring is a region of high electron density. An electrophile is electron-deficient and is therefore attracted to that cloud, which is why benzene reacts readily with electrophiles.

The reaction stops at SUBSTITUTION rather than going on to addition because replacing a hydrogen leaves the delocalised sextet — and with it the large resonance stabilisation of about \(150\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) — intact, whereas an addition product would have to give it up.

The same high electron density REPELS a nucleophile, which is itself electron-rich. In addition, benzene has no leaving group and its \(\text{C}-\text{H}\) bonds are strong, so nucleophilic substitution takes place only with great difficulty and under drastic conditions.

(i) From ethyne — cyclic polymerisation. Three molecules of ethyne passed through a red hot iron tube at 873 K polymerise to benzene:

\(3\,\text{CH}\equiv\text{CH} \xrightarrow[873\,\text{K}]{\text{Red hot iron tube}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\)

(ii) From ethene — first convert it to ethyne, then cyclise:

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2} \text{CH}_2\text{Br}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr} \xrightarrow{\text{NaNH}_2} \text{CH}\equiv\text{CH} \xrightarrow[873\,\text{K}]{\text{Red hot iron tube}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\)

(iii) From hexane — aromatisation. \(n\)-Hexane passed over a catalyst of \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3\) (or \(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\) or \(\text{Mo}_2\text{O}_3\)) supported on alumina at about 773 K and 10-20 atm undergoes cyclisation with loss of four molecules of dihydrogen:

\(\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[773\,\text{K},\ 10\text{-}20\,\text{atm}]{\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3/\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + 4\,\text{H}_2\)

Hydrogenation only adds two hydrogen atoms across a double bond; it does not change the carbon skeleton. So every alkene wanted must have the skeleton of 2-methylbutane, \(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\), with a double bond placed on one of its carbon-carbon links.

Numbering the parent chain C-1 to C-4 with the methyl branch on C-2, the possible positions are C1-C2, C2-C3 and C3-C4 (a double bond to the branch methyl gives the same compound as C1-C2):

\(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\) 2-Methylbut-1-ene

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\) 2-Methylbut-2-ene

\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2\) 3-Methylbut-1-ene

These three alkenes all give 2-methylbutane on hydrogenation.

An electrophile attacks the ring most readily when the ring is most electron-rich, so groups that withdraw electrons (such as \(-\text{NO}_2\)) deactivate it and the more of them there are the slower the attack.

(a) Chlorobenzene has no nitro group, \(p\)-nitrochlorobenzene has one and 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene has two.

Order: Chlorobenzene > \(p\)-Nitrochlorobenzene > 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene.

(b) Toluene carries only the electron-releasing \(-\text{CH}_3\) group and so is activated; \(p\)-nitrotoluene carries one activating \(-\text{CH}_3\) and one deactivating \(-\text{NO}_2\); \(p\)-dinitrobenzene carries two deactivating \(-\text{NO}_2\) groups.

Order: Toluene > \(p\text{-}\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{NO}_2\) > \(p\text{-}\text{O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{NO}_2\).

Toluene undergoes nitration most easily.

Nitration is an electrophilic substitution by \(\text{NO}_2^{+}\), so it is fastest when the ring carries the highest electron density and when the positively charged arenium ion intermediate is best stabilised.

The \(-\text{CH}_3\) group of toluene releases electrons by the inductive effect and by hyperconjugation, so it raises the electron density of the ring and stabilises the intermediate — toluene is activated relative to benzene.

Benzene has no substituent and is the reference.

The two \(-\text{NO}_2\) groups of \(m\)-dinitrobenzene withdraw electrons strongly by both the inductive and the resonance effect, so the ring is strongly deactivated and nitration is hardest.

Order of ease of nitration: Toluene > Benzene > \(m\)-Dinitrobenzene.

Anhydrous ferric chloride, \(\text{FeCl}_3\), can be used in place of anhydrous \(\text{AlCl}_3\).

Like \(\text{AlCl}_3\) it is an electron-deficient Lewis acid, so it accepts the chloride ion from ethyl chloride and generates the ethyl carbocation that attacks the ring:

\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{FeCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5^{+} + \text{FeCl}_4^{-}\)

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. FeCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{HCl}\)

Anhydrous \(\text{FeBr}_3\), \(\text{BF}_3\) or \(\text{SnCl}_4\) serve the same purpose.

In the Wurtz reaction two molecules of an alkyl halide are coupled by sodium in dry ether, \(2\,\text{R}-\text{X} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{R} + 2\,\text{NaX}\), so a single alkyl halide can only give an alkane with an EVEN number of carbon atoms.

To obtain an odd-numbered alkane two DIFFERENT alkyl halides must be taken, and then the two alkyl radicals couple in all three possible ways, giving a mixture of three alkanes with closely similar boiling points that is difficult to separate. The yield of the wanted product is therefore poor.

Example — preparation of propane from bromomethane and bromoethane:

\(\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + 2\,\text{NaBr}\)

but alongside the propane the same mixture also yields

\(2\,\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_3\) (ethane) and \(2\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\) (\(n\)-butane).

Hence the Wurtz reaction is not preferred for alkanes containing an odd number of carbon atoms.
